language_wrapper: Let prime p = {prime_p}. For each positive integer x that is divisible by p, define g_p(x) to be the greatest power of p dividing x. For each positive integer n, define S_n = sum_{k=1}^{p^{n-1}} g_p(p k). Determine the greatest integer n strictly less than {bound_n} such that S_n is a perfect {k_power}-th power.
hardness_rationale: The seed reduces to S_n = 2^{n-1}(n+1) and a square test. Here, we generalize to any prime p and to perfect k-th powers. This forces solvers to derive S_n = p^{n-1}((p-1)n + 1) via counting p-adic valuations, then to analyze when a product of a high p-power with a linear term is an exact k-th power. Handling general k and the p-adic contribution t = v_p((p-1)n + 1), including the case when p divides the linear term (which happens for n in specific residue classes modulo powers of p), substantially raises the difficulty: one must track exponents modulo k and ensure the non-p part is a k-th power. This is a deeper use of valuations and congruences than the original square-only, base-2 case.
notes: Proof sketch: For each k between 1 and p^{n-1}, v_p(pk) = 1 + v_p(k). Counting numbers with exact p-adic valuation j in 1..p^{n-1} yields (p-1)p^{n-2-j} for 0 <= j <= n-2 and 1 for j = n-1. Thus sum_{k=1}^{p^{n-1}} p^{v_p(pk)} = sum_{j=0}^{n-2} p^{1+j}(p-1)p^{n-2-j} + p^{1+(n-1)} = p^{n-1}((p-1)(n-1) + p) = p^{n-1}((p-1)n + 1). Write A(n) = (p-1)n + 1. Let t = v_p(A(n)) and M = A(n)/p^t with gcd(M, p)=1. Then v_p(S_n) = (n-1) + t and for any q != p, v_q(S_n) = v_q(M). Therefore S_n is a perfect k-th power if and only if M is a perfect k-th power and (n - 1 + t) is divisible by k. Since p does not divide (p-1), t equals the largest a >= 0 such that n ≡ r_a mod p^a where r_a ≡ -(p-1)^{-1} (mod p^a) (unique by invertibility). In particular, t=0 unless n ≡ r_1 mod p. This characterizes all solutions n < bound. The verifier implements exactly these conditions without constructing huge S_n, and the generator ensures nontrivial instances (either k > 2 or p > 2 and at least one solution with t > 0).
source_question: For each even positive integer $x,$ let $g(x)$ denote the greatest power of 2 that divides $x.$ For example, $g(20)=4$ and $g(16)=16.$ For each positive integer $n,$ let $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{2^{n-1}}g(2k).$ Find the greatest integer $n$ less than 1000 such that $S_n$ is a perfect square.
